summary: Gives a mission statement for the IETF, defines the terms in it, argues why such a statement is needed, and records some of the debate that led to it.

plainLanguage.summary: Every team needs to be able to say in a sentence what it is for. This memo writes down that sentence for the people who make Internet rules.

questions: what is the ietf mission statement
what are the ietf cardinal principles
what does rough consensus and running code mean
subtitle: The IETF's one-sentence goal, its mission, and the five principles it promises to follow.

tldr.problem: The IETF has to make decisions, sometimes without asking the whole community, and it had no short written statement of what it is for to judge those decisions against.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3935 states a goal (make the Internet work better), a mission (produce high quality, relevant technical documents) and five cardinal principles, defines the key terms, and records the debate over scope.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 95) that gives IETF leaders a yardstick: does a proposal help, hinder or ignore the mission? The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 3935 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 95), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Goal and the Mission
sections.content:
The memo opens with a one-line goal: to make the Internet work better. The mission says how: the IETF produces high quality, relevant technical and engineering documents that influence the way people design, use and manage the Internet so that it works better.

Those documents include protocol standards, best current practices and informational documents of various kinds. Note the split the RFC makes later between a mission (what an organization sets out to do), a goal (what it hopes to achieve by doing it) and activities (the specific actions it takes).
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is the big wish: make the Internet work better. The mission is the job you do to get there: write good, useful instructions that people can follow.

sections.title: The Five Cardinal Principles
sections.content:
The IETF promises to pursue its mission in adherence to five principles.

  • Open process: any interested person can take part, know what is being decided and be heard. Documents, working group mailing lists, attendance lists and meeting minutes are made publicly available on the Internet.
  • Technical competence: the IETF produces documents only on issues where it has the competence to speak, listens to competent input from any source, and expects its output to follow sound network engineering principles.
  • Volunteer core: participants and leaders come because they want to further the mission of making the Internet work better.
  • Rough consensus and running code: standards rest on the combined engineering judgement of participants and their real-world experience implementing and deploying specifications.
  • Protocol ownership: when the IETF takes ownership of a protocol or function it accepts responsibility for all aspects of it, even aspects rarely seen on the Internet. When it is not responsible for something, it does not try to control it.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the club rules. Anyone can join in, you must know what you are talking about, people come because they care, you decide by what most of the experts agree on plus what really works, and if you adopt a protocol you look after all of it.

sections.title: Terms the Statement Depends On
sections.content:
The RFC defines the words it leans on. The Internet is a large, heterogeneous collection of interconnected systems used for many kinds of communication. It includes the core Internet (ISP networks) and the edge Internet (corporate and private networks, often behind firewalls, NAT boxes and application layer gateways).

A standard is a specification with a unique identifier where the IETF has agreed that if you want to do this thing, this is how to do it. It does not mean the IETF mandates or polices its use. Its benefit is interoperability, so that multiple products can work together.

Participants are individuals, not companies or governments, and they are the fundamental unit of the IETF. Quality means ideas expressed clearly enough that everyone building to them understands them the same way, with the consequences of the design described and beneficial to the Internet as a whole. Relevant means useful to people who make decisions affecting the Internet. It does not mean correct or positive: a report of a failed experiment can be highly relevant, and documents delivered a year after the core decisions are far less useful.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you make a promise you should say what your words mean. Here a standard is a recipe everyone agrees to follow if they want their gadgets to work together, and people, not companies, are who the group is made of.

sections.title: Why a Mission Statement Is Needed
sections.content:
The IETF has to make decisions, and in some cases people acting on its behalf have to make them without consulting everyone first. The RFC points out that getting an informed consensus on a complex subject out of a community of several thousand people in a short time is nearly impossible.

A defined mission gives a way to evaluate alternatives: does this help or hinder the mission, or is it orthogonal to it? When resources are limited, which use serves the mission better? The RFC adds that choosing leaders who are trusted to use good judgement is another step, and one the IETF is already trying to take.
sections.plainLanguage: A big group cannot vote on every little thing. If everyone knows what the group is for, the people in charge can make quick choices by asking, does this help our purpose?

sections.title: Scoping the Mission
sections.content:
Section 4 records the hard questions. On the scope of the Internet, the IETF is not value-neutral: it embraces decentralized control, edge-user empowerment and sharing of resources. It settles on covering protocols and practices for which secure and scalable implementations are expected to have wide deployment and interoperation on the Internet, or to form part of its infrastructure, and it will not lead where it cannot gather the competence to make technically sound standards.

On research, invention and adoption, documents should be judged by different criteria depending on which kind they are, and an experiment showing an approach is not viable may help the Internet more than a competent standard useful only in a few cases. Unbounded research may suit a research group; bounded work may suit a working group.

The mission is not the procedures: the appeals process exists to detect violations of open process and technical competence, and which body declares a document ready for publication is outside the mission. The IETF uses English for its work because of its utility in a global context. On protocol ownership, where the IETF defines a standard that is mostly used off the Internet it keeps administering it, and where it builds on standards from other organizations it works with them and does not try to take them over.
sections.plainLanguage: The group decides which jobs are really its own. It sticks to things it knows about, it does not confuse how it works with why it works, and it does not grab other people's projects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is two sentences. It says that considering security is one of the core principles of sound network engineering for the Internet, and that apart from that it is not relevant to this memo. The RFC defines no protocol, so there is nothing on the wire to attack.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is about how a group works, not about a machine that can be broken into, so the only security point is to remember to think about safety when designing things.

items.title: Open process
items.text: Anyone can take part, know what is being decided and be heard.

items.title: Technical competence
items.text: Speak only where the IETF has the competence; listen to competent input from any source.

items.title: Volunteer core
items.text: Participants and leaders come to further the mission.

items.title: Rough consensus and running code
items.text: Engineering judgement plus real-world implementation and deployment experience.

items.title: Protocol ownership
items.text: Own all aspects of what you take on; do not control what is not yours.
